newsitem.title: FRANCE: ATHLETICS-JOHNSON SUFFERS FIRST DEFEAT SINCE 1989.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-JOHNSON SUFFERS FIRST DEFEAT SINCE 1989.

text.p: Michael Johnson crashed to his first 400 metres defeat for eight years when he came back from injury to race at the Paris grand prix on Wednesday.
The world and Olympic champion, who pulled a hamstring in his 150-metre showdown with Canadian Donovan Bailey on June 1, had not lost in 56 races over the distance since 1989.
Fellow American Antonio Pettigrew won the race in a time of 44.86 seconds in damp weather at the Charlety stadium with Davis Kamoga of Uganda second in 45.19.

Johnson, who won both the 200 and 400 titles at the Atlanta Games last year, could only finished fifth in 45.76 after storming into an early lead which he held until the runners hit the final straight.
The American left the stadium immediately after the race without talking to reporters.

His trainer Clyde Hart said: "We didn't know where we were with conditioning. Speed was not a factor as he is usually out in front after 200, but, when you lay off for a month from running and almost two from your last 400, it shows."
Hart said he and Johnson had to review their plans and see whether they would continue on the European circuit or go home.
Bailey put young American pretenders Maurice Green and Tim Montgomery firmly in their place with a commanding victory in the 100 metres.
The Canadian world and Olympic champion made light of the drizzle and coolish conditions to win in 10.07 seconds.
"The weather isn't good but I always like to come to Paris and win the 100," Bailey said.

Green and Montgomery finished first and second at the U.S. national championships two weeks ago with impressive times of 9.90 and 9.92 respectively, sounding a warning to Bailey ahead of the world championships in Athens in August.
Montgomery was second in 10.12 with fellow Americans Brian Lewis (10.19) and Green (10.23) third and fourth.

Namibia's Frankie Fredericks, second to Johnson and Bailey respectively in the Olympic 100 and 200 metres, took the 200 easily with Trinidad's Ato Boldon -- the fastest man this year over 100 -- way back in sixth place in 20.75.
Local favourite Marie-Jose Perec, the women's 200 and 400 metres Olympic champion, disappointed her fans by coming in a poor seventh in the shorter sprint.
When she alluded afterwards to it being her first race of the season and said she was only just getting over a stress fracture of the shin, she was met with a cacophony of whistles.
This was in marked contrast to the applause for winner Inger Miller of the United States whose time of 22.48 seconds equalled the year's best. Perec clocked 23.17.
In-form American Bryan Bronson won the 400 metres hurdles for his second successive win over Olympic champion and compatriot Derrick Adkins.
Bronson ran the third fastest time of the year, 48.15 seconds, easily beating Zambia's Samuel Matete (48.93) into second place. Adkins was third in 48.96.

Mark Crear won the 110 hurdles for the third successive year in Paris in a photo finish with fellow American Allen Johnson, the Olympic champion, who said: "When I was last here two years ago it was also a photo finish between Mark and me."
The constant drizzle made world record attempts very difficult. Ethiopia's Haile Gebrselassie ran well short of his own 5,000 mark when he clocked 13 minutes 1.51 seconds after a fast early pace.
Moroccan Hicham El Guerrouj beat his Algerian rival Nourredine Morceli in a stirring 1,500 metres, winning iFRn three minutes 31.87 seconds.
